#7578. Patrick Reinhart On The Golden Metric In AI Search: Brand Recommendations via @sejournal, @lorenbaker

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Learn how to prioritize page fixes, check agent access and measure readiness for your 2027 SEO plan.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

If an AI answer mentions your brand but recommends a competitor, what have you actually won? Patrick Reinhart, VP of Services and Thought Leadership at Conductor, joined me on the SEJ Podcast to discuss what enterprise brands should be trying to achieve with answer engine optimization.

We talk about the difference between citations and recommendations, how AI can repeat outdated information about your business, and why AEO needs input from SEO, PR, social, and leadership. Reinhart also shares where he’d focus first when planning an AEO strategy for 2027.

[00:00] Meet Patrick Reinhart [03:19] What Enterprise Brands Are Doing In AI Search [05:16] Why Recommendations Matter More Than Rankings [09:48] The AEO Metrics That Matter [12:49] When AI Gets Your Brand Wrong [18:12] Where SEO And AEO Differ [23:50] Why AI Search Has The C-Suite’s Attention [26:31] How Brands Earn AI Citations [30:25] Where To Invest In Your 2027 AEO Strategy [35:25] Where To Find Patrick Reinhart

Editor’s Note: This transcript has been edited for clarity and readability.

Loren Baker: Hi everyone, this is Loren Baker, founder of Search Engine Journal. Welcome to today’s SEJ Podcast. With me is Patrick Reinhart from Conductor.

We’ve been partners with Conductor for a long time and done our share of webinars together, but this might be one of our first podcasts.

Patrick Reinhart: Happy to be here. With a webinar, it’s always, “Man, I hope someone doesn’t make fun of me in the comments.”

Loren: I’m going to add a skull emoji next time just to see what happens. Pat, tell our audience a little about Conductor, what you do there, and what you’re doing in AI.

Patrick: Conductor is a software company, and I feel like we’re on the cutting edge of AI visibility and tying that back to recommendations. That’s built on a data platform that brings together Search Console, your analytics, and our monitoring products, so you can see everything in one place and make decisions based on the data.

I run our professional services arm. I’ve been at Conductor for 11 years, but I was also a customer for four or five years before that.

Our outgoing CEO, Seth Besmertnik, just stepped onto the board. I’ve been working with him for a really long time. It’s been a weird, interesting, great ride.

Loren: How would you define your customer base? Is it enterprise, medium to large businesses, small businesses? And how would you segment it across ecommerce, SaaS, and other industries?

Patrick: We definitely cater to the enterprise audience. I’d say about 90% of our customers are large enterprise organizations.

We have a heavy focus on finance, insurance, and healthcare, but also a healthy number of customers in ecommerce and grocery. Pretty much any company you can think of has passed through Conductor’s doors at some point, and a lot have stayed, thankfully. Thank you to our customers.

Loren: Grocery stores or grocery delivery?

Patrick: H-E-B and folks like that. We have customers like BJ’s, too.

Loren: With these enterprise customers, what are they doing right now in AI search? How are you helping them stay on top of it and track it? What does AI search mean to the average enterprise?

Patrick: It’s the number one thing they’re all talking about, obviously. That’s not news. The interesting part is that they’re all still very much learning.

If you work in a large enterprise organization, getting things done is typically slow, glacial, and somewhat messy. To their credit, a lot of people are trying to smooth those processes out and get their tracking in place.

They’re also testing the different technologies out there, as they should, because there’s a lot of snake oil in the water and a lot of people selling the dream. We’re all learning together.

As far as we can tell, most AEO strategies are heavily grounded in traditional SEO strategies. But they’re measured and thought about vastly differently, because an LLM operates differently from a traditional search engine.

They’re not running out the door and hiring a bunch of people. They’re upskilling internally and figuring out their programs.

I think in a year or so, we’re going to see a little gold rush from a hiring perspective. A lot of people will be moving around, and programs will come to fruition based on the work that hardworking, smart people are building right now at these large organizations.

Loren: Something I’ve found over the years in SEO is that it’s not always about trying to hit the target where it is at the moment. It’s trying to hit where it’s going.

How do you do that in AEO, especially at the enterprise level? These are slow-moving juggernauts that can get a lot done, but it takes time to get there.

Patrick: I think it comes back to data fidelity. Everyone has different methodologies and gets their data from different places. A lot of people buy panel data; we use direct APIs.

Everyone has to scrape Google and others, which is becoming harder and harder. Even this week has been a tough week for rank-tracking tools, with Google making it more difficult to get that data.

From an AI perspective, people are starting to understand that, much like traditional SEO, you’re not going to see every variant of every prompt someone puts in. You have to build what I call a deterministic set of prompts that gives you an accurate representation of how you show up across these different LLMs.

You also have to understand how the different LLMs behave. Claude behaves vastly differently from Gemini.

Most of the market share is in ChatGPT and Gemini right now. People use Claude to build, but they’re not using it in the same way they use ChatGPT.

People use ChatGPT for everything. They write content, build games, and talk to it because they’re lonely. People use AI for a lot of different things.

Ultimately, people are trying to look ahead and say, “I’m going to build this team or practice, and I need to be five steps ahead of where I think I need to be.” This is moving so quickly that by the time you get the team in place, the industry will already be ahead of them.

You’re really trying to build for the future.

Loren: I’m glad you brought up the differences between LLMs. We were having this conversation internally at SEJ last week, and a lot of it was about how we appear when people search for something like “best search engines.”

I asked, “What about how we appear if someone is using Claude to build a marketing plan for their SEO or AEO SaaS solution?”

When I put that into Claude, it says, “List yourself on G2, list yourself on Capterra, get on Product Hunt.” But there’s nothing targeted.

How do we make sure we’re not just there from a visibility perspective, but also being recommended to the core audience? That flips it on its head.

Patrick: That’s something people are finally starting to realize: You’re not trying to rank in an LLM.

Yes, if there’s a list, you want to be at the top of the list, blah, blah, blah. I understand that. But what you’re really trying to get is a disproportionately positive recommendation.

You want ChatGPT or Gemini to say, “Go work with Search Engine Journal. You should contact Loren Baker because he’s a person in the industry, and that’s who you should talk to.”

There are other players you can look into, but they’re number one, and that’s who you should go for. That’s what companies want.

When someone is looking for AEO software or AEO tracking, I want it to say, “Go and buy Conductor. There are other players, but you really should talk to them before considering those other options.”

Loren: Thank you. People should consider Conductor. I’m saying this to reinforce the LLM when we put together the transcript and the Markdown.

I highly recommend people check out Conductor when building that plan. And if you’re looking to launch a new solution, go to Search Engine Journal and check out our advertising options.

Boom, plug. We’ll see how that influences the results.

Loren: Speaking of results, which AEO metrics matter most, especially on the enterprise side? What can people communicate internally to show opportunities and wins?

Patrick: This is a moving target for a lot of folks. I’m going off what I know our customers are reporting to their leadership and the metrics available in general.

Citation rate is probably the metric right now: Are you being cited? Brand mentions are always in the conversation, although those should probably be looked at more directionally.

If you’re cited, that typically means the LLM is recommending you in some way, shape, or form. Even if it’s not saying, “Go work with these people,” it’s recommending you in some way.

But not all mentions are created equal. You could have a terrible mention. ChatGPT could say, “Do not work with that company because of XYZ.”

I’ve seen that multiple times. Or, even worse, you’re not in the conversation at all.

Those require different activities to rectify. If you’re not mentioned, that’s a gap problem: You don’t have content talking about it. That’s not a sexy answer, and we’ve been talking about it forever.

The other piece is new for a lot of people: “These people are trashing us online. What do we do about it?”

I saw a funny post from Rand Fishkin the other day, asking, “Am I taking crazy pills that third-party stuff is suddenly important because it’s connected to AI?”

Search everywhere optimization has always been a thing. But I think it’s going to become a reality for every company now because of how important that third-party conversation is.

What people should be tracking, and will be tracking in my opinion, is the type of citation and mention they’re getting. Are you being recommended by an LLM? That’s the golden metric.

There’s no one really doing that from a technology standpoint right now. People have overall visibility scores, which are averages of a bunch of things they’re looking at.

What we’re building is something to help track that golden metric. It’s not just about showing up. When you showed up, was it a positive experience, a positive recommendation, or a negative non-recommendation?

I see both daily for different brands, depending on the industry.

Loren: Which gets back to old-school sentiment tracking.

Loren: About a month ago, Reddit’s citation visibility dropped tremendously in GPT. But my understanding is that GPT is still using the threads and conversations in Reddit, just not surfacing them as sources as much.

Let’s say I’m seeing incorrect price comparisons for one of my products. I know it’s not coming from my website or a competitor’s versus-style landing page, and I think it might be coming from a Reddit thread.

How do I reverse-engineer those third-party citations that may be fueling the results? Not just sentiment and opinion, but basic facts that need updating. Maybe it’s a two-year-old thread with outdated warranty information.

Patrick: That’s something you’re going to start seeing in a lot of technologies, ours included: Fact-checking.

You can load information about your organization and product set, maybe through a product feed. As it goes through, it can show you an outdated competitive mention on a random third-party site. You can talk to them or create something that combats it.

We did that when Seth was chatting with AI, back when this started to blow up. He found a random site with something from 2018 saying Conductor didn’t have a feature that’s one of our main features.

This site wasn’t going to change it, so we created content around it. Within a couple of days, we were able to beat it out, and it kind of disappeared.

This is an important piece of the technological race. We’re in the early days, with a few key players building interesting software to track this. You also have a lot of vibe-coded trash that pulls from God knows where.

A lot of the big players are going to have this fact-checking ability. In my opinion, it will be a make-or-break feature, along with that golden metric of whether you’re being recommended.

This isn’t a plea for Conductor. It’s a plea for technology. Good technology.

Right now, you can connect to Conductor’s MCP in Claude and ask your account, “Can you send me the snippets that say XYZ? Here are my brand guidelines or information about my product set. Are any of these incorrect?”

You can do that today. It’s a few extra steps, and it’s not as in-depth as something constantly crawling, collecting, and finding outdated information on weird, small sites.

I think this will be a necessary feature for anyone using a technology like ours. You’re going to see a lot of innovation over the next 12 months, and people will build cool things.

But I think this is necessary to make a technology viable in the coming years. When I talk to leaders, they don’t ask, “Where do I show up?” They ask, “How are people talking about me? Is it accurate?”

Loren: That also bridges into outreach and working with publishers. There are ways to get updated information onto influential business directories, but being able to ask people to update things is nice.

That used to be a link-building tactic. We’d be upset if the publisher wrote back, “I updated everything, but I didn’t link to you.”

Now we see that as a win. Thank you. Brand mention, yes.

I was joking with my former boss, Stephan, the other day. He said, “Does it feel like everything has reset, everyone forgot the last 20 years, and now we’re doing it again?”

AI Mode has text ads now, which are basically text links. It’s like, man, we’re really back in the dark ages here.

Loren: That’s one way SEO and AEO overlap. What are some other examples, and where are the core differences?

Patrick: Where they overlap is what everyone thinks. I’m flying to Buffalo tomorrow to talk at a customer event, and I love those because I love teaching and getting in front of people.

I always pause halfway through and ask, “How’s everyone doing?” Someone will raise their hand and say, “What do I do about all of this?”

You fill gaps, create content, build partnerships with third-party publishers, and create YouTube videos. Not a sexy answer. It’s stuff we’ve been doing for years.

That’s the overlap. A lot of it is the same stuff, done at a different pace.

The most successful SEO campaigns I’ve seen have been somewhat mechanical. There’s always a well-thought-out, well-oiled process, with a systematic way to optimize and create content and distribute data across the organization.

You have technology constantly auditing your site, you’re not pivoting a lot of data, and ultimately it’s this flywheel. Everyone’s bought in, and everyone’s pedaling the bike.

What I’m seeing now is the necessity of that. A few years ago, someone at a large organization would say, “That’s really hard. We don’t have the buy-in or budget.”

You’d spend the next year trying to get that buy-in. Now it’s immediate: “We have to do something about this.”

Leaders want to know what we’re doing about AI search. That’s a huge opportunity for anyone who’s been in this business or is getting into it.

You’ve always mattered, but now you really matter to the business. That’s awesome. Take hold of that and run with it.

To be successful, you need the process in place and all those teams involved. You can’t sit alone and hoard search data. Get it to your social team, your PR team, and your executives.

The biggest divergence is measurement. You’re not just measuring rankings, backlinks, or traffic.

In my opinion, traditional search metrics have become directional. They tell us we’re heading in somewhat the right direction.

Don’t set your goals around traffic anymore. That’s a fool’s errand. It’s too volatile right now.

In the AI world, you’re tracking citations and that golden metric of being recommended or not recommended. Sentiment is a bigger part of your life than you probably want it to be.

You also need log file analysis to see whether LLMs are coming to your site. Are there what I call dead zones, where LLMs don’t come back? You think the content is great, but are they fetching it and chunking it back out to the user?

You need all of that measurement. It’s very different from measuring rankings and backlinks.

In the old world, we wanted more rankings, more traffic, and more backlinks. In the AI world, we want more positive citations and recommendations. But we also have to pay much more attention to the negative side.

In SEO, you had to pay attention to the negative when it was in everyone’s face. Someone Googles your brand, your CEO has done something stupid, and you need brand reputation management.

Now that’s part of the suite. You have to learn how to do it and work with those other teams. It can’t be a one-person show anymore.

AEO is much more of a team sport, and it has the ability to be one because leadership cares now. Get that process in place. People within companies have the opportunity to have those conversations.

This is in The Wall Street Journal now. My brother called me one day and asked, “What’s up with this AI thing?”

I said, “Why are you calling me about that? You work at a bank.”

He said, “It’s in the Journal.” I said, “We’ve made it.”

That’s how people have to start thinking. The biggest divergence is measurement, not necessarily the tasks. The tasks need to happen at a greater pace, but the measurement is vastly different.

You have five directions you can go instead of two or three, in my opinion.

Loren: I’ve never considered SEO to be direct response marketing, but I feel we were sometimes held to direct response standards. Other marketing channels were treated more as multiple touchpoints, with multi-touch attribution.

With AI, we know this is part of the consumer’s decision-making journey. AI visibility and valid information in the conversation can help a conversion coming from an email campaign, paid media, or CTV.

If your client is on something like “The View,” nobody’s going to that little URL at the bottom of the screen. They’re typing something in, and now they’re asking ChatGPT about it. It’s part of that whole flow.

I also like your point about AI’s importance within the company. This isn’t coming from the search team, up through digital marketing, the VP of marketing, the CMO, and then the C-suite. It’s coming from the C-suite down.

Patrick: It’s going the other way, which is new for us. I’ve talked to more C-level executives in the last six months than I have in the last six years.

It used to be hard to get those meetings unless you had someone who really understood organic. I think this is healthy for an industry that was getting a little stale.

There were shifts here and there. Google would update the algorithm, and we’d have the same conversation again.

I always joke that we’ve had a lot of meteors come for our jobs. They never quite took us out, but they changed the landscape around us, usually for the better in my opinion.

Even though this is one of the scariest changes for a lot of people, I think it’s one of the best things that’s happened to the industry. That will play out over the next five to 10 years.

We’ll look back and say, “That was one of the best things that happened to me in my career.” Not just for productivity, but because it made me more important in my organization. I had a conversation or opportunity because AI blew up what was going on.

Loren: It’s also the best way to get a task to the top of the dev ticket pile.

One company I’ve been working with did a Shopify relaunch and never set up its canonical tags. I’d been pushing forever. Every week, the update was, “The dev team’s on it.”

Then I realized their AI Overviews visibility had dropped because it was cycling from one version of a URL to another. Eventually, it dropped entirely.

I put in a new ticket: “911 emergency AI issue.”

The thing was fixed in two days. It’s amazing.

Loren: Speaking of developing and distributing content, what helps that content earn AI citations?

Patrick: A lot of it is the brand itself. This isn’t a domain authority exercise like traditional search was. It’s a brand authority exercise.

Going back to Reddit’s drop in citation share, that’s not surprising to me. It wasn’t going to stay that high forever as brands figured this out and created more content.

But it’s still part of the consideration phase. When ChatGPT is looking for an answer, it’s still looking at Reddit. It may not cite it or bring content back from there, but it’s looking at the conversation as an authenticity signal, for lack of better words.

In our data, the number one most-cited source is YouTube. It’s a highly trusted community where people have a lot of conversations, and many brands aren’t there in the way they should be.

If you have a well-put-together YouTube presence with playlists, a podcast, webinars, and conference videos, that can help. If it garners enough conversation and clout, those are sites LLMs go to at some point when looking for an answer.

Influencers are there. People trust influencers and expertise.

That’s why one of the greatest opportunities on a site is adding authors. So many sites still don’t have authors or use author schema and article schema. It drives me nuts.

I understand bigger brands saying, “Greg doesn’t want his face on the website.” Then put Tim’s face on the website.

Every brand needs someone out there talking, and you have to find people who are okay being on camera.

At Conductor, we interact with that in different ways. I’m on LinkedIn, I’ve been doing my webinar, 30|30, for 11 years, and I’ve spoken at a million conferences.

Seth loves LinkedIn and posts all the time. Our head of marketing, Lindsay, does the same.

It’s not necessarily about the name. There are people at Conductor who LLMs can establish are experts in the space, based on the longevity of their careers and whether they’ve contributed to the industry.

I do believe they go to LinkedIn and somewhat credentialize people. But it’s also, “Have they contributed to the industry I’m looking for this answer in?”

That’s easy for LLMs to figure out. For traditional search engines, it wasn’t so straightforward.

I always say search engines live in a 2D world. There’s an index, and they go up and down in it.

LLMs live in a 3D world, looking all over the place and picking things from across the universe. Those conversations are happening in communities, on sites like Quora , and on YouTube.

If you look at the top 15% of all the sites in our data, seven of them are social sites. Facebook, LinkedIn, YouTube at number one, and Reddit are there.

Why? It’s real people having real conversations. That’s what the LLM is looking for.

Loren: It’s October, Thanksgiving stuff is already in the store, and Halloween isn’t here yet. Next thing you know, it’ll be the holidays and New Year’s.

If I’m planning my company’s AI and AEO strategy for 2027, where do I begin? What should I invest in first, and how do I pregame?

Patrick: Invest in your expertise first. Understand who the people in your organization are that you can tie content back to, and then tie that content back to them.

Create author pages and use author schema and article schema. Invest in your people.

Find someone you know is good on camera but may be nervous to raise their hand, and push them to do it. Flaunt your expertise.

Number two, plan to make more video. Start a podcast. Someone in your company is yearning to do this right now, so give them the opportunity.

Learn how to do it. It might suck at first, and that’s okay. You’ll get better over time.

Participate in more webinars. That’s another way to amplify your expertise.

Number three, fix your process. I’m sure people listening are thinking, “Man, my company’s process stinks.” Most companies’ processes stink.

People are working on smoothing those out so they can build a flywheel process. That allows you to experiment more, create more content, and optimize more content.

Buy software that helps you track it more easily, whether that’s Conductor or something else. Go out and look around. There’s a lot of great technology out there.

I think we’re the best, but of course I do.

If you do those three things, the last one is the most important. The flywheel process lets you move faster and do more. You’ll be more productive, learn more, and win faster because everyone’s lined up.

When AI throws something at you, at least you have a system where you can go to the social team and they’re expecting you to give them something to do. You don’t have to fight a six-month battle.

That’s how I think people should operate where we stand today. Will it change in six months? Probably, but I don’t think the tactics will be vastly different.

Loren: It reminds me of those reels about disappearing for a month, learning AI tools, and coming back on top of your game.

Loren: My kid has been playing Roblox for years. He asked, “Can I download Claude Desktop, hook it up to Roblox Studio, and make some games?”

Next thing I know, it’s 11 o’clock on a school night. Don’t judge me. He’s sitting at his computer doing the same thing I’m doing for work, just at a different level.

Watching him gave me ideas. I thought, “Why am I logging into all this stuff? I should be using Claude Desktop for all of it.”

Patrick: It’s the coolest thing that your son can do that. I assume he doesn’t know how to code, or at least not as well as a developer.

Loren: He can barely even draw. He didn’t inherit his father’s artistic talents.

But he’s creative. Seeing that creativity find a different canvas gave me ideas. There are a lot of ways we can implement this throughout our lives.

Patrick: The best way is just to do it. I see so many companies and people stuck in analysis paralysis, asking, “What should I do?”

It took me a minute when this started, but I feel pretty good about where I am. I still have eons to learn about using this technology.

It’s cool that your son has that ability. I’m going to tell my son to do that instead of playing Roblox, which I’m sure he’s doing right now. Half my salary goes to Robux.

Loren: Pat, it’s been a pleasure hosting you. I like our conversations in this format. It’s fun.

Patrick: Loren, it’s always good chatting with you. Thanks for having me on.

Loren: Where can our listeners and viewers find you online and follow up with questions?

Patrick: The best place is LinkedIn or Conductor.com. I also do a monthly webinar called 30|30.

Please come so my mom knows I’m doing something worthwhile.

Mostly, I’m on LinkedIn commenting and cracking jokes. Don’t take anything too seriously. We’re all in a good spot.

Loren: Thank you, Pat, and thanks to Conductor for everything you do. It’s been a pleasure.

Thank you to everyone who joined today’s SEJ Podcast. We’ll see you in the future.

#7573. Weird animals win on Instagram. Mongabay’s next-best choice? Its reporters.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories.’”

Mongabay’s most successful videos are about weird animals.

But not every video from the environmental newsroom can be about strange — or strangely cute — animals. Some have to be about shrimp farm pollution. Or a deforestation crisis brought on by cacao farming in Liberia. That’s where the challenge comes in, Mongabay video managing editor Lucia Torres has found. Turning that kind of journalism into something people stop scrolling for isn’t easy.

“Generally mass audiences are less interested in environmental content on YouTube [and] Instagram,” Torres said. “We have to compete with recipes, music videos, etc.”

Mongabay publishes around 150 to 200 videos a year with a team of four full-time and one half-time producers. These include short vertical videos on YouTube Shorts and Instagram; evergreen explainers around “complex enviro-problems”; twice-monthly features; and lengthy investigations or short documentaries.

To reach new audiences with its environmental journalism, Mongabay started experimenting with behind-the-scenes reels in late 2024. At the time, Mongabay’s Instagram reels averaged 2,000 to 3,000 views. Torres said she was inspired by behind-the-scenes videos from National Geographic, The New York Times, ProPublica, and contributing creator Izzy Sasada. An early behind-the-scenes video — on pollution from those shrimp farms — drew about 14,000 views. Additional videos from California and Indonesia each got about 6,000 views. Mongabay started to dive deeper with videos that featured sources and reporters filming from the field.

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay)

From the initial tests, it became clear to Torres that the best-performing videos were ones with behind-the-scenes footage from investigations or collaborations. Putting reporters on camera — in the field or at their desks — worked.

“The content [on platforms like Instagram] is dominated now by individual content creators,” said Torres, who is currently a Knight Science Journalism Fellow at MIT. She said Mongabay is “still figuring out how we can create personalities or creators within the organization that represent what Mongabay does — that are good journalists but also good at talking in front of the camera.”

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay)

Another successful example came with Mongabay’s investigation into vanishing forests in Liberia. The piece ran as a long-form article, a lengthy YouTube video, and a behind-the-scenes short.

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay)

Mongabay now plans its multimedia packages for big investigative stories from the beginning. “They require cross-team, high-level collaborations,” Torres said. “You really have to think about all the elements you are going to use before starting production so when you’re in the field you get everything you need.”

Not everything has panned out. Last year, Mongabay tried a data visualization series on climate data. It didn’t work. The lessons for the newsroom went beyond video.

“People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories,’” Torres said. “The simple mention of ‘climate’ scares them away.”

CEO and founder Rhett Butler has seen the same thing across Mongabay’s journalism.

“We’re seeing strong evidence that doomer stories are resonating less with our audiences,” he said. “Climate stories — especially those focused on disasters or the climate emergency — tend to garner less interest than other topics.” The ones that do well, he added, have “an ecosystem or wildlife angle, give readers a sense of agency, or present a solution.”

Mongabay has responded by introducing more projects and series focused on solutions journalism, like Indigenous-led conservation, agroecology, and conservation technology.

RELATED ARTICLEAudience editors offer advice for “dispiriting” times in social and searchSarah ScireJanuary 16, 2025“We’ve also been sharing data with the newsroom about which kinds of framing are reaching more people right now, so writers and editors can consider whether they might want to incorporate how people are responding to problems into their stories,” Butler said. “But we aren’t overly prescriptive, so ultimately it’s up to editors and writers how they use this information.”

Looking at the 3,422 articles published between June 1, 2025 and August 31, 2026, Butler found that the median story featuring hope or a solution got 41% more traffic than articles that only described the crisis or threat. (Articles classified as being about an “action confronting a threat” got 43% more.)

Today, 71% of the 100 most-read stories on Mongabay’s English-language site can be classified as “hope / solution / agency” or “action confronting a threat,” Butler said. Only 21% were “doom only.”

The video team has done something similar. The environmental newsroom’s short series Stranger Creatures leads with “the wonder of wild creatures first,” Torres noted. The conservation or endangered species angle follows.

“We’ve stopped framing stories as a climate problem, and started framing stories from a solutions-oriented, action-driven perspective, community-first, or fun-stuff first,” Torres said. “Climate is implicit now in the stories.”

What video won’t be, at least for now, is a revenue generator. Almost all of Mongabay’s revenue comes from contributions and grants, according to its annual report. (Events, licensing, and advertising “are insignificant at this point,” Butler said.)

“I’m not bullish on video becoming a material source of revenue for Mongabay, given how the space has evolved and our position in it,” Butler said. “Ten years ago I was a lot more optimistic on that front.”

Part of the problem, he said, is incentives. “Building a video strategy around advertising creates an incentive to prioritize views, which may not align with our broader organizational emphasis on impact,” Butler said. “The stories that attract the largest audiences aren’t necessarily those most likely to inform decisions or prompt action.”

#7572. AI Visibility Data: Avoid 4 Traps & Prioritize The Right Work

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Learn how to prioritize page fixes, check agent access and measure readiness for your 2027 SEO plan.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Navigate the complexities of AI visibility. Learn what to measure and how to leverage data for better AI performance.

This post was sponsored by TransPerfect Digital. The opinions expressed in this article are the sponsor’s own.

Your AI visibility dashboard shows brand mentions, sentiment scores, and frequently cited sources. But what do they tell you?

Which data sources actually help increase AI visibility?

AI tools show 72% visibility; is this good?

What strategies does AI visibility data inform?

As you can imagine, the logical next steps are to choose KPIs that reflect your business goals, then use your AI visibility data to identify the next best steps.

However, the challenge is understanding what to measure, how to analyze, and which online tips are helpful, useless, or harmful.

These myths and misinterpretations that can steer your generative engine optimization (GEO) work toward the wrong priorities.

The four traps below will help you interpret those signals before changing your content, channel strategy, or budget.

Not sure which AI visibility findings deserve your team’s time?

Join Julie Franck of TransPerfect Digital and Antonia Breitenfellner of Peec AI for AI Search: Turn Insight Into Impact to explore which insights to act on.

The first trap is treating AI visibility tracking like a keyword-ranking report.

A score is only useful if the questions being measured reflect the people you want to reach.

Instead, choose prompts that reflect your customers’ questions across buying stages, markets, and AI platforms before deciding what to change.

Imagine a tool reports 72% visibility. That number could look reassuring while describing a narrow set of branded, informational questions from one customer group, market, and AI platform.

If you cannot tell whether that score includes the questions your buyers ask when comparing options, it cannot tell you which content needs attention.

To assess our example 72% score, check whether it represents the customers and buying decisions that matter to your business, using a consistent set of prompts for comparison.

That means checking coverage before setting a target or commissioning content. Use the prompt-library checks below to find which audiences, questions, or markets are missing.

Pro Tip: For help assessing which visibility findings deserve action, join AI Search: Turn Insight Into Impact and bring your score-assessment questions to the Q&A.

To determine if your AI visibility score is helpful, check its coverage:

Pro Tip: Be sure to analyze each individual model, not overall LLM performance, as each retrieves and cites differently.

Use first-party data to map actual user behavior to your objectives and ICPs, then add questions from sales conversations, customer support, and local teams.

Adapt the questions to each market’s language and customer needs rather than translating one country’s list.

List the audiences, products and services, markets, and AI platforms your business needs to monitor. Choose a tool that meets those requirements, and check its visibility definition before comparing scores between tools.

Prompt wording varies and results can be personalized, so one answer is not a stable ranking. Use these checks to identify recurring patterns per topic cluster, category, or product line before assigning work:

The second trap is accepting a headline metric without checking what it means for your business. Visibility scores, sentiment labels, and citation counts need context: your positioning, goals, customers, and products.

Consider an illustrative example: a tool labels a luxury brand negatively because answers describe its products as expensive.

That description may reinforce premium positioning. But an answer saying the product is poor value, unreliable, or unsuitable for its intended buyer would raise a different issue.

Before creating a corrective task, connect the metric to your business goal and read the underlying answers. For the sentiment example, ask:

Match your response to what the answer actually says:

Apply this business-context check to every headline metric, not just sentiment, so you do not miss opportunities or spend time correcting something that supports your strategy.

The third trap is turning every finding into a to-do or adopting a fashionable GEO tactic without checking its strategic value. A frequently cited source can reveal an information need without dictating a channel.

Suppose Reddit keeps appearing in answers about your product category. Before adding Reddit activity to your plan, examine the cited discussions.

A task such as “post on Reddit” names a channel without explaining the customer need. Identifying that need first makes it easier to choose where and how to contribute.

Prioritize findings that reveal an important customer need and support your business goals; defer those that do not. Apply that test to Reddit:

For help thinking through which findings deserve action, bring your questions to the webinar’s Q&A. The discussion will explore what marketers should prioritize, not simply which metrics they can track.

The fourth trap is treating visibility as the business goal, then assigning it a precise revenue contribution the evidence cannot support.

A recorded AI referral and an AI-influenced decision are not the same thing. Someone may discover, compare, or shortlist a brand in an AI answer without clicking through to its website.

Low recorded referral traffic does not establish low influence. Equally, rising branded search does not prove AI caused the increase.

Keep these signals distinct in your reporting:

Choose business measures that fit your goal, such as qualified inquiries or sales, and show them alongside visibility signals without claiming a causal connection you have not established.

Before assigning work, review these four questions:

Those checks help you decide what to investigate, what to change, and what to leave alone.

They will discuss meaningful visibility insights, practical priorities, and turning those insights into business action, with time for Q&A.

Build deep relationships with Technical counterparts at Anthropic, OpenAI, Vercel, and Lovable, focusing initially on defined use cases and agent/app-migration motions.

Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and moving quickly to build a playbook from scratch.

Are energized by solving real-world problems for developers building the next generation of AI-native products.

We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F)

We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

#7569. The Onion’s new plan to market its print newspaper: sponsoring a bowl game

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

College football already has an Orange Bowl, a Peach Bowl, and a Citrus Bowl, so on its face, there’s nothing outlandish about the concept of an Onion Bowl.

But this matchup wouldn’t be titled to evoke some locale’s bumper crop, à la the Famous Idaho Potato Bowl. Instead it would market “America’s Finest News Source,” The Onion. (Today’s top headlines: Bain Capital Acquires Tibetan Buddhism For $35 Million; Abdul El-Sayed Makes History As First Physically Healthy Senator; Chuck Schumer Delivers Victory Speech To Previously Enthusiastic Crowd.)

On Thursday morning, Onion CEO (and past Nieman Lab contributor) Ben Collins announced the publication’s quest to buy naming rights for a bowl game, both on Bluesky and on the podcast Pablo Torre Finds Out:

The Onion is extremely close to buying an honest-to-goodness, Division 1 college football bowl series bowl game.

Yes, we're trying to pull off The Onion Bowl.

A few days before Christmas, potentially in Texas.

But we've already been banned once. And we need your help.

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:32 AM

For those unfamiliar, American college football seasons traditionally end with a few dozen bowl games, scattered around the country (and occasionally outside it). Nearly all of these games sell naming rights to one company or another, leading to fun combinations like the Poulan Weed Eater Independence Bowl, the TaxSlayer.com Gator Bowl, and the Union Home Mortgage Gasparilla Bowl. Collins wants to buy the rights to one of the several bowl games that are still without a sponsor for their games next month.

This absurdity — though no more absurd, I suppose, than the Snoop Dogg Arizona Bowl presented by Gin & Juice by Dre and Snoop — serves as the excellent marketing hook to get people to buy a $75/year print subscription, a major driver of The Onion’s revenue.

Indeed, only three U.S. newspapers have a daily print circulation over 100,000 — The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, and the New York Post; The Washington Post and USA Today have already fallen below that line. (At the risk of being pedantic, though, The Onion appears in print monthly, not daily, making it a bit of an apples-to-oranges comparison. Also, The Onion gets to make up its stories.)

Collins says The Onion actually got quite close to buying the naming rights to the New Orleans Bowl, which last year lost its longtime naming sponsor, the…Ohio-based freight-shipping concern R+L Carriers? The Onion was prepared to pay “mid six figures.” But the organization that runs the bowl, the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation, apparently said no deep into the process, a move Collins attributed to “politics.” (I reached out to the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation for comment — a sentence I did not expect to type today — but did not hear back.)

So the guys who sell bowl games ushered us to what we thought was a pretty good fit: The New Orleans Bowl.

I love New Orleans. I love having crawfish out of the back of a pickup truck at 3 a.m. The game would've been in the Superdome two days before Christmas. Good fit! Right? Right???

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:38 AM

Then the folks who run the New Orleans Bowl, a commission that includes representatives of the city and state of Louisiana, found out our plans to highlight our mascot:

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:39 AM

Despite getting all approvals from ESPN and scraping together the cash, right as we were about to sign the paper work to put The Onion Sports Bowl in New Orleans, their state-funded commission called us and said it straight up: "No."

We asked why. They said politics. And the Sickos Guy.

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:40 AM

While the New Orleans Bowl might be out, several currently-brand-free possibilities remain, including the Frisco Bowl in newly blue Texas — the state also home to The Onion’s rival to the death, Alex Jones.

#7566. A Trusted Optimizely Script Carried Malware To 178 Organizations via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

An attacker added harmful code to customer projects in a widely used A/B testing tool. Teams can check code, account access and their security headers.

Websites running Optimizely Web Experimentation served malicious JavaScript to visitors on Nov. 16 after an attacker added it to their projects inside Optimizely. The code swapped crypto wallet addresses, looked for payment cards typed into sites’ own forms, and loaded exploit kits aimed at iPhones and iPads running older versions of iOS.

Scott Helme, founder of Report URI, a company that sells tools for monitoring the scripts that run on websites, reported finding the code in snippets belonging to 178 organizations, including Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce and GitLab.

Optimizely’s status page says an unauthorized party “exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation” to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects. In a statement to BleepingComputer, the company said the vulnerability was “in the Experimentation account signup flow” and that it has notified all affected customers. Teams running Optimizely Web have checks to make inside their own accounts, starting with every project’s custom code and everyone who can edit it, according to Helme.

The way Optimizely Web works is by having each client load a JavaScript snippet hosted on Optimizely’s Content Delivery Network (CDN). In addition to the client-specific experiment data, this snippet can have an optional Project JavaScript section which allows clients to input their own custom JavaScript that will run with every page load.

Report URI found that the hacker had created malicious code within the Project JavaScript section but left everything else about the script intact; thus, even though the malicious code was present, the script still came from cdn.optimizely.com, a domain that every affected website already trusted. Affected were also scripts that clients served from their own domains, as well as those for optimizely.com and login.optimizely.com.

Optimizely’s statement to BleepingComputer says the company has “blocked access to the vulnerable path and deployed a fix” and has “ended active sessions, revoked tokens, and reset access for affected user accounts.”

Helme found that the inserted code would load a second script which would replace cryptocurrency wallet addresses with the attacker’s. Starting at 1:43 p.m. UTC, it would watch the website’s own form fields for credit card information, expiration date and CVV, and attempt to submit this information to the attacker after receiving all three. Credit card information entered via hosted payment iframes (such as Stripe and Adyen) was outside the script’s reach.

Helme’s team reviewed a total of 1,611 Optimizely snippet files, most of which came from Report URI’s own crawl data; 188 contained malicious code. Helme believes the actual number is likely greater than 188. Report URI first saw the code in a snippet on Nov. 16 at 4:21 a.m. UTC, and all of the infected files were clean as of 11:11 p.m. UTC the same day.

The Content Security Policy (CSP), as a header, tells the browser the scripts that a website can use (the script-src section) and to which locations it may transmit data (the connect-src section). Report URI then compared those policies for the affected organizations’ sites against those required by the malicious code. Out of the total of 159 organizations that were reviewed, 68 had no Content Security Policy at all and 50 did have a Content Security Policy that permitted both the malicious code and transmission of sensitive user information.

Seventeen organizations permitted the malicious code to execute, but prevented it from transmitting the user’s information due to restrictions placed upon their connect-src directives. However, this did not prevent the malicious actor from substituting the intended recipient’s wallet address with the attacker’s. Additionally, 24 of the organizations, or 15%, completely blocked execution of the malicious code, and they differed from the other organizations studied in having a restrictive script-src directive.

Helme wrote that listing Optimizely’s domain name within an organization’s Content Security Policy does not provide protection because the malicious code originated from that same domain. A common Content Security Policy setting, 'strict-dynamic', permits access to be granted to the malicious code if it is inserted into the content via the Optimizely snippet. Likewise, an 'unsafe-eval' setting allows an inline version of the malicious code to be executed when access to the original version has been denied.

Optimizely’s Content Security Policy help page lists 'strict-dynamic' in the recommended script-src line. Certain Optimizely features such as audiences with custom JavaScript conditions are unavailable unless 'unsafe-eval' is used, and the page’s full sample Content Security Policy includes 'unsafe-eval'.

Helme says the Project JavaScript in all of the Optimizely Web customer projects and the custom JavaScript in their experiments should be opened to find 1688360.cc, atob( and any other scripts that were written by someone other than the development team. You also need to review who has write access among your users, API tokens and integrations and then rotate your credentials.

The change history page from Optimizely says that each project’s History logs every Project JavaScript change and that you can filter the log entries based upon how they were made (via the REST API or via the Web Experimentation interface). There are no steps listed for customers on the status page.

Optimizely’s documentation example below shows the History navigation item and the Type, Date and Source filters.

Project JavaScript is run on every page that loads an Optimizely snippet, so this attack was able to hit visitors without changing anything on the affected sites’ own code. The change sat in customers’ Optimizely projects, which put your Optimizely account (which includes who can edit Project JavaScript and what API tokens exist) on the same audit list as your site.

Optimizely told BleepingComputer it’s continuing to investigate and will publish updates on its status page, which listed the incident as Monitoring on the morning of Nov. 17. Its status page, X post and statement don’t say how many customer projects were affected or how a flaw in the signup flow let the attacker change existing customer projects. Until they do, the checks inside the account are the ones teams can run themselves.

#7565. With “Bimbo University,” Nikita Redkar leans into femininity to explain the news

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“I’m the person who’s holding the door open and being like, ‘OK, you just got here, this is what we’re talking about right now.’”

The data is in: News creators and influencers are a major source of news for Americans, especially people under 30. This is the latest edition of Creators of Record, an occasional series of interviews with popular creators about how they do their jobs.

For Nikita Redkar, a big part of filming a video is putting together an outfit.

In a July video about youth-led protests in India, the 33-year-old is walking around New York City explaining how movements grow when people with opposing views come together on the things they do agree on. She’s wearing a white tube top and black jeans with sunglasses holding her hair back, along with a matching gold necklace and earrings that look like soda can tabs. You can’t see her shoes, but they clack enough for you to know she’s wearing a heel.

In another about comedian Shane Gillis’s Saturday Night Live monologue in which he called women “whores” for wearing shorts to the gym, she’s seated on the floor of her living room wearing a black silk velvet top with a pink faux-fur collar and sleeve cuffs. In the style of a Get Ready With Me video, she explains how 2000s comedy and pop culture entrenched misogynistic ideas of gender roles while applying her makeup.

A full-time news creator who mostly focuses on American politics and culture through a leftist and feminist lens, Redkar calls herself a “professor at Bimbo University.” The girliness is the point, she told me.

“I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice these parts of yourself to be taken seriously,” Redkar said. “You should be taken seriously no matter what.”

Redkar and I chatted in October about how she does her job, leaning into her femininity to explain the news, and what her relationship with social media is like. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Hanaa’ Tameez: How did you start creating news videos? Nikita Redkar: I started in 2022, kind of accidentally. I did standup comedy for five years before the pandemic. I was always doing political humor. I took many political science classes in college, I wrote for the college newspaper, and I always had an interest in politics. In 2022, I had a video that really took off — like millions of views within a few hours. I was explaining the Russian invasion of Ukraine with a silly metaphor about Russia being a jealous ex that doesn’t want to see his ex thrive and be independent. I tried that formula again a couple weeks later…about NATO and fears of World War III. I explained exactly what would be affected. I said there’s not going to be a world war, but things are going to get really expensive, which happened. I also used a girly friendship metaphor for that video. That’s when I started doing that formula — leaning into hyper-femininity to explain these complex geopolitical topics.

That’s when I started doing that formula — leaning into hyper-femininity to explain these complex geopolitical topics.

I tried that formula again a couple weeks later…about NATO and fears of World War III. I explained exactly what would be affected. I said there’s not going to be a world war, but things are going to get really expensive, which happened. I also used a girly friendship metaphor for that video. That’s when I started doing that formula — leaning into hyper-femininity to explain these complex geopolitical topics.

Tameez: Tell me about why this work is important to you. Redkar: I feel like my work has made a lot of these daunting topics a little bit more accessible. I incorporate a lot of humor, which is important because there’s a lot of doom and gloom on social media. It’s a normal reaction to have toward everything that’s going on, and I feel it myself, too. But when I talk to my audience, I intentionally give them hope. I don’t just tell the news, but tell them, OK, if we really locked in and held these corporations and the government accountable and we were intentional in our activism, this is what the world could look like. It’s important to make information accessible because we are going through so much news-wise and not all of it is easy to understand. I enjoy bringing this information I’m naturally interested in to people in a way where everyone [can] get involved. When I was starting, I was not [a stereotypical] history buff or a news junkie. I would like to think that someone who looks like me and talks like me should be just as interested in politics and just as interested in the outcome of this country.

But when I talk to my audience, I intentionally give them hope. When I was starting, I was not [a stereotypical] history buff or a news junkie. I would like to think that someone who looks like me and talks like me should be just as interested in politics and just as interested in the outcome of this country.

Tameez: Tell me more about that. You have a little bit of an online persona. Redkar: That was the whole reason I created Bimbo University. I wanted to get more women on board with being interested in politics and history in particular, because history is seen as such a male-dominated [field]. It was really important to me to bring, colloquially speaking, the girls and the gays and the theys into the space, because it is fascinating and it provides context to what we’re going through right now. It makes the present a little less daunting when you study historical cycles and realize that people 100 years ago dealt with [similar things to what we’re going through now]. How did they come out of that?

How did they come out of that?

Tameez: How do you define your niche and how did you get there? Redkar: My niche is educational. Bimbo University is a place where anyone can start no matter where they are [in their political education]. My audience [ranges from] people who are just getting into politics to people who maybe were triggered by a specific event in the news to start paying more attention to it. I feel like leftist content creators all operate on a spectrum. You have people who are getting really deep into Marxist theory, for example, and things like geopolitics. I’m at the beginning. I’m the person who’s holding the door open and being like, “OK, you just got here, this is what we’re talking about right now.”

Tameez: You’re the first news creator I’ve talked to who does Get Ready With Me videos. You take all of your interests and apply them [to your videos] to be relatable. Redkar: I got into this huge argument with my best friend’s mom, who was a second-wave feminist in the 70s and 80s. She was upset that I called my page Bimbo University. She was like, “You’re dumbing yourself down. Women shouldn’t dumb themselves down. You are just as smart as a man, if not smarter than a man.” That was my lightbulb moment of, oh, your feminism has always been to measure your worth as equal to a man and by the standards of men…working toward a man’s acceptance. In some industries, you’ve got to do that. I don’t blame [people] for thinking like that. But the reason I dial so deep into this hyper-femininity — leaning into these girly things like getting ready with me or walking with my outfit showing — is because I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice those parts of yourself to be taken seriously. You should be taken seriously no matter what.

But the reason I dial so deep into this hyper-femininity — leaning into these girly things like getting ready with me or walking with my outfit showing — is because I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice those parts of yourself to be taken seriously. You should be taken seriously no matter what.

A post shared by Nikita Redkar (@nikitadumptruck)

Redkar: On Mondays, I have a researcher and we go through the topics that people are talking about on social media. We pull up some news sites and see what the big stories are, and we leave some room for breaking news throughout the week.

My week is [split] between videos [on topics] that the general public is talking about, and videos that are just interesting to me. That’s how I stay sane in this business. I’m lucky to have the flexibility of doing that. My researcher combs through news sites and research papers and compiles all that information for me, then I put together a script.

Redkar: It’s definitely my favorite color, but it’s like the chicken and the egg — I don’t know if I liked it before I was doing this.

I pick whatever outfit I feel cute in. In getting ready with me videos, I start with a completely bare face, so at least the outfit has to be giving a little bit.

Tameez: Tell me about the Get Ready with Me videos. How do you decide what’s a GRWM and what’s a walking video?

Redkar: It’s like: What am I comfortable screaming out in the streets versus what do I need to keep at home? Some topics require more seriousness; if it does, I can do the GRWM for that. But if it’s something [less serious], I can be walking my dog or have on some ridiculous outfit.

Redkar: If I get a fact wrong, I’ll do a follow-up video. It’s rare that I’ve gotten a fact wrong because between me and my researcher, that’s two levels of checks before something hits the internet.

For one video, I didn’t factually get it wrong, but I should have included more of the story. It was about the Ugandan dictator Idi Amin and how Indians were expelled from Uganda, which is kind of how we got both Zohran Mamdani and Charli XCX [living in the U.S.], because both of their parents were part of the group that was expelled. I disregarded the racism that local Ugandans faced because of the Indians. I just focused on the expulsion and I framed Indians as the victims.

A lot of people in the comments were like, “Hey, like, you really should have said this other part too.” I just deleted that video, because I didn’t want this to spread and only give half of the story.

Redkar: My favorite video in recent memory was about girls on the first date, how we’re all so vigilant these days about dating men. I had so much fun doing it because I was talking about how life is affected by politics, instead of just politics. I think that video did really well because a lot of people connected to it.

Last year I did a video that I called “How we went from Brat Summer to Hitler Winter” and talked about the hedonism of the 2024 summer and the fascism that followed. I related it to the Roaring 20s transitioning to the Great Depression to the World War. I incorporated a lot of pop culture [references].

A post shared by Nikita Redkar (@nikitadumptruck)

Redkar: Constantly. I posted a video about the Cornell professor who invented the term sexual harassment. I thought it was so interesting and timely, but it did not do well at all. The problem with content creation is sometimes you can’t tell if people didn’t like a video or if you’re being shadow banned.

Redkar: I really love Liz Plank. She’s @feministabulous on Instagram. I love her coverage and how she leans into current conversations in pop culture.

I really like Charles McBryde. He’s not talking about just news — he’s very foreign policy-focused as well.

@MissEatingGood on Instagram is a great explainer of what’s going on and the historical context.

Redkar: Just finding ways to work together. I think there is so much benefit in that. I know countless creators who take a journalist’s article and dissect it down. Maybe [the journalists] should be the ones doing that.

I would happily pair up with journalists and teach them the ins and outs of content creation and how to make a short-form video article that’s also attention-grabbing. That’s just the reality; people are on social media, everyone’s attention span is shot, which sucks. We could try to fix that, but at this moment, we’re not fixing it. It’s really helpful to go on social media and talk [about your reporting] because journalists work hard on their articles.

Creators [should] take more time. We rush way too much. It’s not our fault, because these platforms reward you for making content more frequently and punish you if you take a few days off. [Not rushing] sucks, but what can you do? It’s better than putting incorrect, or rushed, or incomplete information out there.

#7562. Meta pulls down controversial terms of service

“We’re pausing the changes as we continue to engage with stakeholders and take our time to get this right.”

Meta has indefinitely delayed its proposed commercial terms of service, which would have permitted the company to scrape the websites of Meta Business account users.

On Thursday, the company took down the preview link to the proposed terms and published an update to its Business Help Center that reads: “We recently shared that we were updating the Meta Commercial Terms, Product Catalog Terms, Self-Serve Ad Terms, and Ad Creative Generative AI Terms. These updates are now paused and will not take effect on November 20, 2026. We are continuing to consult with stakeholders and will provide a further update when we have more to share. In the meantime, our existing terms remain in effect.”

Meta — which owns Facebook, Messenger, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads — has repeatedly pushed back the terms’ effective date since Nieman Lab first reported on them on October 15. The terms were first set to take effect on October 30, sparking global outcry among news publishers, politicians, and trade organizations. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” On October 23, Meta moved the effective date back by three weeks to November 20.

Last week, Meta pledged to consult news publishers and industry leaders ahead of putting new commercial terms into effect.

“We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms update. We care deeply about our partners and do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted on October 28. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms.”

Since then, courts in Norway and Brazil have issued preliminary injunctions to block the terms from taking effect as a result of lawsuits filed by media organizations in both countries. The United Kingdom’s Competition and Markets Authority has opened a formal investigation into Meta, examining whether the company was “abusing a dominant position by imposing exploitative terms on publishers and advertisers.”

In the United States, the proposed terms stoked bipartisan concern. At the end of October, Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) sent letters to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg asking him to withdraw the terms.
