#7509. How I’m Approaching AI Search (And How You Should To)

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Learn how to prioritize page fixes, check agent access and measure readiness for your 2027 SEO plan.

Where search leaders are putting 2027 budget, plus the AI visibility scorecard that replaces session reporting.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Forget citation hacks and obsessing over prompts. AI search is an opportunity to rethink how we approach marketing, audiences and discoverability.

AI is strangely simple. And we’re overcomplicating it.

In focusing on citation tactics and cheap visibility tricks, we’re missing the bigger picture. As an industry, we’ve got away with poor content for years. Updating the same “best spoons” article three times a week because some other idiot is doing exactly the same thing.

There’s nothing inherently wrong with it. It’s just too SEO-y. We’re missing a much bigger opportunity by framing it through a really narrow lens.

I don’t have the energy or the wherewithal to play catch-up every year or two. So I think of AI search as the ultimate synthesis of your marketing efforts.

Your positioning, reputation, expertise, content, and presence across the internet are all potential inputs into how AI systems understand and represent you.

It’s not just about your website anymore.

I’ve spent a lot of time recently working on AI search, information retrieval, audience research, and discoverability strategies. The more I do, the more convinced I become that we need to approach this as marketers, not SEOs.

But don’t build your entire “marketing” strategy around it. I use marketing in the loosest possible sense of the word.

If you’re in dire need of a refresher, here’s a few parts on the fundamentals of modern information retrieval:

There’s one other concept I haven’t written about in detail: query fan-out. Not because it’s not important, more just because a) it’s pretty dull and b) it isn’t a new concept for SEOs. We’ve been using tools like AlsoAsked for years to understand related questions, adjacent information needs and the wider context surrounding a search.

But we also need to distinguish between three things:

They’re related, but they aren’t interchangeable. Being crawled doesn’t guarantee inclusion in training data. Being retrieved doesn’t guarantee a citation. And a citation doesn’t guarantee commercial value.

Understanding these mechanisms is important – mainly just so you can answer the brain-dead questions people ask you about AI. Building your entire marketing strategy around their current implementation is the action of a halfwit.

Models, retrieval systems, and interfaces will change. An owned audience is a considerably more durable investment. So build one.

This is the biggest change I’ve made to my approach. Not just for AI search, but for traditional SEO.

I don’t begin by asking which prompts a brand should appear in. Or how much search volume a keyword or even topic has. Mainly because my trust in search volume and all forms of visibility is at rock bottom.

So I use SparkToro to investigate where audiences spend time, which websites they visit, who influences them, and which platforms they’re disproportionately likely to use compared with the wider population.

For this audience, I know that if I want to influence them, LinkedIn is a non-negotiable (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett)

I combine that with traditional search research, AI search behaviour and an assessment of the brand’s existing positioning. You don’t need to overcomplicate this – ask a number of different LLMs about insert brand and record the responses.

I want to answer some relatively straightforward questions:

First, our owned platforms. We use what we’ve learned to improve the way we position ourselves, the services we offer, the language we use, and the content we create.

Let’s try to make things under our control as human and well-targeted as possible.

Second, our wider marketing strategy. We identify the publications, communities, creators, platforms, and people capable of influencing that audience, and decide how to reach them.

Audience affinity with specific Subreddits, via SparkToro (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett)

You need to know this. Not because it might get your brand mentioned as part of the training data. But because this is where you should be marketing.

Made-up prompt data is out. Real, human-led marketing is in. If we want SEO to be taken seriously, this is the proper evolution.

The goal isn’t to manufacture mentions for an AI model. It’s to build a brand people want to discover, engage with, and recommend.

If those activities also increase your representation in AI systems, wonderful. But that’s a delicious byproduct, not the reason for doing them.

While audience research informs the wider strategy, your website needs to be accessible, understandable, and representative of who you are. That is something reasonably competent SEOs can lead.

Can the relevant search and AI crawlers access your content? Can they render it? Are you inadvertently blocking systems you want to reach?

This means reviewing bot management, robots directives, rendering, indexability, internal linking, site architecture, and the usual technical SEO fundamentals.

A traditional SEO-type audit with a few improvements.

One that understands that not all AI bots serve the same purpose. Training crawlers, search crawlers, and user-triggered retrieval systems can have different access requirements and commercial implications.

Crawlers do different things (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett)

Especially important if you’re working for – or with – a publisher. Someone whose business may depend on you understanding the wider context.

Most large publishers block AI crawlers, sometimes almost indiscriminately, under the banner of copyright protection. There may be very good commercial reasons for doing so. But those decisions fundamentally change your discoverability strategy.

If you’re restricting access to your content, you need to understand what you’re giving up, what you’re protecting, and where the value might exist instead.

Perhaps that’s content licensing, direct audience relationships or proprietary products.

The role of the SEO changes considerably in an environment where you’re not maximising access. You’re helping the business understand the trade-offs between visibility, intellectual property and commercial value.

It’s like a paywall. You’re restricting reach for commercial purposes. It’s the correct move if played properly.

See Cyrus Shepherd’s excellent test to understand how much search traffic was truly influenced by Google’s AI proposition.

This is where I think modern information retrieval methods and SEO intersect perfectly. I’ve written about how to approach this in Entities Are the Foundation of Modern SEO.

This isn’t about adding some structured data and hoping ChatGPT tries to hump your leg. Spoiler: It won’t.

It’s about making sure that your owned presence accurately represents your positioning and that the wider internet provides credible, independent evidence to support it.

So, we know who we are. We’ve represented ourselves properly. Now we have to rely on *shudders* other people to corroborate this message.

This references a podcast I did with Andy Francos and an article I wrote for Lumar two years ago (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett)

We’re talking actual, real marketing (not SEO). PR, partnerships, content and audience development.

If the people you’re trying to reach spend their time reading particular publications, following particular experts or participating in particular communities, those are the places worth investing in.

Bollocks to a citation. Your audience is there. You know, people you could actually sell something to.

That might mean publishing original research, collaborating with influential people, appearing on podcasts, creating genuinely useful resources or contributing expertise to relevant publications.

Some of those activities will generate links. Others will generate mentions, relationships, conversations and brand demand – a real representation of site quality in Google.

The more consistently you’re associated with the right subjects, people and organizations, the stronger your wider digital presence can become. That is, in essence, how training data and entity relationships work.

If you’re lucky, some of that evidence may eventually influence how AI systems represent you.

But you won’t care, because you’ll have been making sales by marketing to actual customers.

Modern methods of information retrieval across SEO and AI search share many, if not all of the same fundamentals.

Arguably, AI search has a longer tail to it. But it’s not sustainable, nor sensible, to create a page for every possible thought your audience may have. To perpetuate a false Henry Ford quote:

“If I had asked people what they wanted, they would have said faster horses.” H. Ford, Never

So you need to strike a balance. No one cares about visibility without impact. At least not for long.

There is room to try and test things. Good things. Things real people will care about.

People like Jan-Willem Bobbink and Dan Petrovic highlight some really brilliant things you can test that are eminently sensible for SEO and AI search. Surprise, surprise, they work for people too. It’s marketing.

Let me give you an example. Maybe more accurately, let me steal one of Jan’s:

“I spent the last three weeks on SEO / GEO work for B2B clients, and the changes that made the biggest difference were mostly about information that was missing or hard to find. Buyers run into the same problems on these sites, so you can usually get these fixes approved without having to explain SEO to anyone.”

Being explicit, consistent, and accurate is not an AI hack. It’s just pretty sensible.

Adding pricing pages, case studies, and telling people why you are the best in the business are always good ideas. Even if your pricing pages just say something like prices starting at x, that is a better way of finding the right audience.

And if you want to feature in AI responses, for god’s sake don’t hide your case studies. You need to provide a clear reason for your inclusion. Hard if your best work is hidden.

Statements like “Client Y saw a 30% improvement in deliverability metrics” can noticeably improve your citation rate because a model is literally looking for a reason to include you. You need to give them one. Just as you would a person.

Experience. Expertise. Authority. Trust. Not so stupid after all.

Measurement’s been broken for a decade anyway. It’s just nice for the C-suite to have numbers to report on – even if they’re complete hokum.

You try and figure this out (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett)

AI visibility’s not much better. A hugely flawed metric given the personalization, lack of prompt data, and completely individual prompts. But it’s better than nothing. Indicative at best, but you need to use something.

People still want to know how they’re represented in AI systems. And so they should – it’s a valuable channel. My preference is to establish a representative set of prompts across four areas:

Track these consistently across the systems that matter to your audience.

Look at whether you’re mentioned, how you’re described, which competitors appear, and which sources are being used. Find out when you start to appear for certain terms and see if it matches your positioning.

I always track my mentions with Alertmouse (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett)

I appear in AI recommendations around news SEO expertise despite having done nothing specifically to optimize for AI search.

What I have done is spend years working in the industry, publishing, building relationships, contributing expertise, and establishing a reasonably clear on-site and off-site identity.

Not a bad list, although I am not sure ChatGPT is quite nailing the profile pictures for us… (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett)

I guarantee you, if you ask Barry Adams, he’ll tell you he’s done nothing special for AI either.

I’ve written what I think are high-quality articles on third-party websites and podcasts, featured in roundups, and built my own distribution platform. It just also happens to work for featuring in AI systems.

AI systems don’t necessarily need to send you traffic to influence commercial outcomes. Which is a good thing, because ChatGPT sends less than 1% of Google’s traffic.

Similarweb’s research found that users who received a brand recommendation in ChatGPT were 2.5 times more likely to visit that brand’s website within the following seven days than users who were recommended a competitor.

Much of that activity happened through subsequent branded searches rather than direct AI referrals. One of those measures of site quality that should be monitored.

AI search can and does function as a brand discovery and consideration channel. I think referral traffic is, at best, a secondary measure of success from LLMs. While they’ve engineered the exit out, you cannot deny the reach these systems have.

Unfortunately, our attribution systems can’t cope with “I saw it here once.” We need to focus on incremental change. The outcomes attributable to marketing.

Establish a baseline. Run a campaign. Measure changes in branded demand, direct visits, conversions, leads, and commercial outcomes. Compare with appropriate benchmarks or control groups where possible.

Keep tracking AI visibility, referrals and citations, but use them as supporting indicators.

Our objective is to establish whether said marketing activity is creating additional business value, not whether ChatGPT has linked to your homepage.

For businesses whose models depend on monetizing information and attracting a click, AI search presents a very different challenge.

They are monetizing other people’s work for their own ill-gotten gain. That is an irrefutable commercial dilemma. Hence all the protectionism. So we need to establish what that cost is and try to find alternative methods of monetization.

In The Generative AI Report Sucks – Let’s Make It Brilliant, I outlined how publishers can combine AI visibility data with traffic dependency, commercial value, audience resilience, and server logs.

We can go some way toward solving actual business problems.

Always, always, always a good thing to do. Regardless of your job.

This opportunity is no different, especially for organizations (like publishers) with substantial authority across particular subjects. They have influence within the wider information ecosystem.

That influence can have commercial value.

Publishers Should Think About AI Visibility. Content licensing, data partnerships, research collaborations, and other commercial arrangements offer opportunities to monetize expertise and proprietary information.

Selling links or undisclosed editorial influence is not a sustainable AI strategy. It introduces reputational, editorial, and search-policy risks.

The more sustainable opportunity is to understand the value of your existing content, expertise, audience, and distribution – and build legitimate commercial products around those assets.

Lots of companies are selling or actively considering selling their archived assets or data to AI companies:

For publishers in particular, this is an opportunity to rethink the value they create beyond the click. See the Daily Mail’s approach to GEO monetization here.

If you’re more on the glass half full side, you’ll be able to sniff out commercial opportunities. Ideally ones that don’t ruin the brand or fall foul of Google’s link payment guidelines.

General advice: If something smells a bit off, it probably is.

If you’re a business looking to take this seriously, there’s an organizational question you need to answer.

Because as great as we can be, it shouldn’t just be your SEO.

This touches technical infrastructure, audience research, brand positioning, content, PR, distribution, commercial partnerships, and measurement. That requires someone who understands the entire ecosystem and, crucially, how to influence people.

Nobody is an expert at all of these things. They’re too different. Too complex.

For larger businesses, I’d be thinking about a Head of Marketing or Head of Discoverability with responsibility for coordinating these activities. Someone who at least knows the basics of each and can herd a clowder of cats.

They need the authority to bring different teams together, allocate resources, challenge existing assumptions and measure outcomes against business objectives.

There’s a reason SEOs rarely graduate to marketing lead positions. We don’t understand wider marketing because we’ve rarely had to. SEO was always the best channel… According to wonky data, anyway.

AI search gives us a very good reason to change that.

And for anyone working in SEO, I think there are three particularly interesting directions.

All three have tremendous value. Limiting yourself to SEO, particularly as a collection of search-engine or LLM-specific tactics, is increasingly short-sighted.

Discoverability has been changing for a decade. We need to think much more broadly about how audiences discover and engage with content. The opportunity is to bring those disciplines together.

A little rebrand and refocus on what you want from your career may be the best thing you ever do.

Stop trying to engineer your way into an AI response. Build a brand worth recommending, an audience worth owning, and a business that benefits whether the citation comes or not.

Enjoy yourself. This will be a better era for marketers and marketing. Your competition is lazy and inept. They’re just faster.

SEO Director at The Telegraph with a decade of experience. Unskilled jiu-jitsu guy. Average chess player. Jack of many things.

#7506. After gutting newsrooms, McClatchy plans to rebuild itself around AI

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

The local journalism that has long powered the 169-year-old company is no longer a viable business model, executives told McClatchy employees during a virtual town hall this month.

Two months after McClatchy Media laid off more than 90 journalists nationwide, executives at the storied local newspaper chain offered a blunt assessment of its future.

The award-winning local journalism that has long powered the 169-year-old company was no longer a viable business model, executives told McClatchy employees during a virtual town hall this month, and its survival depended on a wholesale reinvention — centered entirely around artificial intelligence.

From the rollout of new lifestyle websites that feature AI-generated articles and sponsored content to legal review and finance, executives revealed how AI is now integrated into virtually every part of the company. The demonstration comes after McClatchy, one of the nation’s largest newspaper conglomerates, carried out deep staff cuts in September at the Miami Herald, The Kansas City Star, and more than a dozen other local news outlets. An anonymous “person close to the executive decision-making” told The New York Times the layoffs were not about AI and were instead about “business performance in some areas.”

A companywide blueprint presented during the meeting highlights how McClatchy is systematically outsourcing the infrastructure for local news to AI agents — and rebranding around lifestyle verticals for sports fans, outdoor enthusiasts, and true-crime junkies.

Dubbed “Project Catalyst,” the companywide restructure will create an “AI-native operating model” that takes “repeated tasks off of humans” and embeds AI agents “directly into the daily workflow,” Jeff Dorsey, McClatchy’s chief operating officer, said at the town hall. Dorsey described the initiative as an effort to automate “non-core as well as core functions,” “get rid of things that just don’t offer the same value” they once did, and “provide cash, frankly, to keep the business afloat.”

McClatchy, which operates 29 daily newspapers across 14 states, didn’t respond to multiple requests for comment.

Central to the rebrand is the launch of four new websites: Crime Hunter, a site devoted to “real-life crime and justice”; Saltwater South, which “celebrates the places, people and experiences that make the coastal South unlike anywhere else”; Camp & Country, a “national outdoor destination”; and Student Section, billed as “the home of the college sports fan.”

Each of the sites is “powered by Trend Hunter,” a company McClatchy acquired in 2024 that uses AI “to glean insights into consumer trends” and sell consumer goods like $33.91 rosemary oil “to support a healthy scalp environment,” a $249 red light therapy cap to regrow hair “without the hassle of messy serums” and $34.99 “MAGIC Mushroom Coffee” for “clarity, balance and natural energy.”

Little discussed, however, were the company’s local news ambitions. Kristine Sherred, chair of the Washington State NewsGuild and the food and dining reporter at The News Tribune in Tacoma, Washington, said that she and other journalists were left to wonder “why we were even invited.”

“Our takeaway was that it wasn’t about news,” Sherred said. “The future McClatchy appears to be building does not seem aligned with the mission of journalism.”

The meeting this month offered the clearest roadmap to date about McClatchy’s all-in approach to AI as one of the nation’s largest newspaper conglomerates navigates traffic declines, shifting consumer habits, and heavy debt obligations. It also comes at a critical moment for a media industry that seeks to modernize with AI — technology simultaneously blamed for gutting web traffic and touted as a tool to cut costs.

“There is no sector that has not been disrupted this year by AI — everyone is going through extraordinary disruption,” Hunter said. Through a laser focus on AI-powered efficiencies, he said, the company can turn around its fortunes. “We can win — not with yesterday’s solutions, though.”

For McClatchy, which has undergone aggressive cost-cutting efforts since it was acquired by New Jersey-based hedge fund Chatham Asset Management in 2020, its pivot toward AI-generated content over the last year has been met with internal pushback and, from some readers, ridicule.

In May, journalists at The Sacramento Bee, the Miami Herald, and other McClatchy-owned papers withheld their names from articles that were produced with its “content scaling agent,” a chatbot that repackages human-written news articles at varying lengths for different audiences — complete with reporters’ names.

Similar resistance has played out at other news outlets. Earlier this month, for example, reporters at the Akron Beacon Journal in Ohio withheld their bylines for two weeks to protest a tool that generates AI summaries of articles that, the journalists allege, undermines their work and provides readers false information.

Many news organizations prohibit the publication of AI-generated articles. But for McClatchy, they’ve become a core part of its business strategy and, according to Hunter, a key part of its “company-wide effort to agentify the entire enterprise.” During a contentious virtual meeting in May, Hunter pleaded with skeptical journalists to get on board or find another job.

Anyone at McClatchy can now build AI tools to support their workflows, Rajiv Pant, McClatchy’s chief product and engineering officer, said earlier this month.

“In every one of these, humans are at the command center, they aren’t just checking the technology’s work,” Pant said. “They set the direction, make the calls and own the results. The technology lets each one of them do more of the work that only they can do.”

Trend Hunter content — including AI-generated posts — now appears regularly across McClatchy’s local publications and social media feeds, including articles with little connection to the communities those outlets have historically served. Recent examples include a post about winter “barn jackets” in the Miami Herald and a feature about collegiate football in Texas for the Kansas City Star.

Other posts highlight obscure beauty products and questionable health trends, including how nugget ice “has become the craze worth understanding,” how saunas have “reshaped social wellness,” and “what your poop color, shape and frequency say about your gut health.”

Or, as one Kansas City Star reporter put it, the layoffs have created news websites where it’s “city reporters out, shitty reporters in.”

“They’re trying to kind of go toward these buzzy-type topics instead of local journalism that holds people to account,” said the reporter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity due to retaliation concerns.

Readers, an overwhelming majority of whom are skeptical of AI use in newsrooms, have also taken notice. In a post on X, one social media user wrote that “people want the news” not “AI generated slop.” Another called into question McClatchy’s decision to publish an article — across numerous local news brands — about why the actress Scarlett Johansson “changed her magnesium supplement routine after a spray left her feet feeling dry.”

This AI slop is what McClatchy forced a bunch of its newspapers to publish in unison a few weeks ago. Who needs real human reporters when you can have this? https://t.co/Z82Vg67WtH

— James (@jameslineky) September 10, 2026

Given the rapid spread of AI-generated content online, McClatchy executives see the brand credibility of its legacy publications as a differentiator. Over time, Hunter said, the market will reward trust — and McClatchy is well positioned to capitalize on its local news audiences.

“It is important that we have credible, accurate and relevant content,” Hunter said. “We are not running from our standards, but we’re running toward a new model to help customers make better decisions.”

In recent months, as much as 20% of articles published by McClatchy newspapers were AI-generated, according to data from AI-detection company Originality.ai. (AI detection tools like Originality are imprecise in distinguishing synthetic writing from human-authored content.) Rather than building new audiences, McClatchy’s use of AI-generated content could erode trust among readers, said Jon Gillham, Originality’s founder and CEO.

Such a reality is already playing out in Washington, said Sherred of the Washington State NewsGuild. Sherred’s union went on strike in May to demand “ethical limits” around the company’s use of AI. The guild said in a statement at the time it was negotiating for “freedom to write hard-hitting news stories that take time, and not be punished if we don’t churn out clickbait.”

“We hear this from people in the community all the time: They don’t want short snippets, they don’t want rehashed work and they don’t want AI telling them the news,” Sherred said. “The only way you get high-quality local news is by having high-quality local reporters actually out there making it.”

Less than a week after McClatchy laid off journalists nationwide in September, executives sent the remaining staff an emoji-laced email announcing “fresh talent”: several executives, two reporters and three editors for its “Content Innovation Lab” — the engine behind its new AI-powered lifestyle verticals.

A recent job listing for innovation lab writers notes the “company’s future depends” on an embrace of AI and the innovation lab is its “next-generation approach to content” where emerging technologies are leveraged to “fuel experimentation and productivity.”

“From barbecue to bourbon, water sports to hiking, and golf to college sports, we are going to develop a steady stream of reader-focused, high-quality content for national and regional audiences,” according to the job listing. Producers will use AI to launch new brands “tied to dedicated communities of interest around travel, food, outdoor recreation, sports and even crime.”

The insights into the company’s future editorial direction come on the heels of its steepest staff reduction in years, with layoffs of investigative reporters, government watchdogs, and other journalists focused on local news.

“The city of Tacoma no longer has a city reporter,” Sherred said. “What’s the purpose of a local paper if you have no one covering your local government?”

Hired to lead the Content Innovation Lab is Patrick Stiegman, a 20-year ESPN digital veteran who, during the meeting this month, turned to sports media lingo to describe the goal behind Saltwater South, Camp & Country, and its other AI-powered lifestyle brands. By “cultivating passionate fans” around obsessive lifestyle niches, he said, the company seeks to leverage reader data “and monetization opportunities” to guide coverage decisions.

Perhaps nobody put McClatchy’s pivot in starker terms than Ariel Storch, recently hired to lead an AI-powered rebrand of its video strategy.

“We make entertainment — not content, entertainment,” Storch said during the Nov. 6 meeting. “Think about a late-night show. Nobody tunes in to be informed, they tune in to laugh. The by-product is you leave knowing about a new movie, a new book, a new product.”

Building new audiences is critical as the company works to claw itself out of debt, said Joe Settineri, McClatchy’s chief financial officer. Stabilizing McClatchy’s core business is necessary, he said, for the Content Innovation Lab and its other AI initiatives to be successful.

“Today, most of that profitability is already spoken for because, like most companies, we have a sizable amount of debt,” Settineri said. “Like a loan on a house, we have to pay it down or you lose the house.”

Microsoft Advertising is rolling out rebuilt automated bidding models. Learn what is changing for Target CPA and Target ROAS campaigns and what to review now.

Microsoft Advertising is rolling out what it calls its biggest bidding model upgrade in a decade. The new models use more signals to predict whether an ad click will turn into a conversion and what it might be worth.

Microsoft will apply the upgrade automatically as it reaches more accounts. That means campaigns can start spending differently before you make any changes yourself. Microsoft announced the rollout on November 18 and plans more bidding updates in 2027.

Microsoft says the new models can change how quickly campaigns spend and how closely they stick to your targets. These are the areas to keep an eye on:

A $50 CPA target still leaves room for a campaign to bring in conversions at $40 each, even if it spends its full budget. A max CPC can limit that flexibility. Say you average $3 a click and cap bids at $5. The cap rules out a $6 bid even if Microsoft expects the click could bring in a conversion within your CPA target.

Say you raise your CPA target on Monday and customers usually take a week to buy. By Friday, you know what Monday’s clicks cost, but you may still be waiting on some of the sales. Faster bidding won’t shorten the time those customers take to buy.

Raising a CPA target or lowering a ROAS target can open up auctions your campaign previously passed up. To limit swings in performance, Microsoft suggests making those changes in 15% increments and reviewing each after one conversion cycle. For a bigger change, like switching bid strategies or adding a conversion goal, Microsoft recommends allowing one to two cycles.

Microsoft recommends conversion-based bidding for new campaigns once the account has at least five conversions. Those can come from campaigns you already run. If you’re still gathering your first five, Enhanced CPC is an option.

On LinkedIn, Sophie Westall asked if the same advice applies to low-volume accounts already using Enhanced CPC. Microsoft Advertising Liaison Navah Hopkins replied:

Every account is different so a blanket recommendation still needs to be put to the test. With that said, so long as the account has at least 5 conversions total, the system is smart enough to use that to begin with conversion-based bidding. While we still recommend the 30-day evaluation period and not making too many changes if you’re working with fewer conversions, the system is much more responsive now!

For judging performance, Microsoft recommends around 30 conversions in 30 days at the campaign or portfolio level. A low-volume campaign can reach the end of that first month and still have too few conversions to judge the switch.

Microsoft reported 10% more conversion value per click at roughly the same ROAS after the model upgrade. That result came from August 2026 global Search and Audience Network data for advertisers using Maximize Conversion Value or Target ROAS.

Microsoft also looked at advertisers who switched bid strategies. Search advertisers who moved from Target CPA to Target ROAS saw 8% more conversion value at a similar ROAS. Advertisers who moved from Enhanced CPC to Maximize Conversions with a CPA target saw 18% more conversions at a similar CPA.

If you’re considering Target ROAS, pull up a few recent purchases in Microsoft Advertising and compare the reported values with the order totals. A $40 order and a $400 order can both show up as conversions even if your tracking assigns them the same value. That’s easy to miss if you’re used to checking that purchases are coming through and leaving it there.

Microsoft reported its largest gains from value-based bidding among advertisers who sent actual transaction values. If your purchase goal uses a fixed value, the reported ROAS reflects that estimate. It can move as you sell more or spend less, but it won’t capture a change in how much customers spend per order.

With lead gen, you may need time to get a better read on what a conversion is worth. Two people can submit the same form, and sales may find out a week later that only one is a fit.

Pedro Bailaderia asked Navah Hopkins about sending an estimate at submission and updating it once more information comes into the CRM. Hopkins supported using the Conversions API or offline imports. She also advised setting a ROAS target that reflects the values you send.

If your team is still working out how to value a qualified lead, that’s worth settling before you set a ROAS target. A campaign can hit the target you set while sales is still waiting for more leads it can work with.

If a campaign already brings in the sales or leads you need at a cost you’re happy with, you can give the upgrade some room before changing anything. Keeping your settings steady makes it easier to see how the new models work with the goals and budget you already have.

The rollout may be more useful if you’ve been adjusting targets to get a campaign to spend more evenly. If delivery settles down on its own, you may have fewer reasons to touch those targets during the week. That would leave you freer to change them when the business needs more volume or can afford to pay more for a conversion.

#7502. Election season lifted public radio sites. So did a Supreme Court scandal and license plate drama.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Stations in New Hampshire, Wisconsin, Massachusetts, and Utah all climbed in our regular ranking of public radio stations between July and September.

More than a year ago, NHPR reporter Todd Bookman started asking questions about “an irregular personnel maneuver” involving the chief justice of New Hampshire’s Supreme Court. Bookman’s reporting ultimately became “Exhibit A” in the ethics probe that led to the justice’s resignation in September.

The bombshell resignation news was NHPR’s biggest story in September — and of 2026 to date. The story helped push NHPR up several spots in our regular ranking of public radio websites. NHPR saw visits rise 22% that month, according to Similarweb visit figures compiled by Nieman Lab.

RELATED ARTICLECollaborations and primary elections boosted traffic to public media sites this quarterNeel DhaneshaJuly 29, 2026At the very top of the list, not much moved. The Chicago Sun-Times, owned by Chicago Public Media, held onto the top spot, followed by Gothamist (from WNYC) and Minnesota Public Radio. As Nieman Lab senior writer Joshua Benton wrote when introducing the rankings, which we’ve also done for local newspapers and local nonprofit news sites, not all markets are created equal. Public radio stations serving major metropolitan areas with lots of college graduates have a bigger potential audience than stations serving smaller communities and areas with fewer resources. And, of course, Similarweb provides an estimate; internal metrics may differ. Still, the rankings are a valuable window into some industry-wide trends, and often an opportunity to highlight local news organizations punching above their weight.

Like several public media sites on our list, election season provided a bump to NHPR. New Hampshire held its primary on Sept. 8 and the statewide public radio station saw a traffic boost from results pages and campaign coverage, said NHPR director of audience engagement Casey McDermott. She described September as a solid month, not an outlier. “But what makes September an exceptionally cool case study is that it reflects two fundamentals at the heart of our mission: a commitment to fresh, local reporting and a renewed internal investment in digital publishing,” McDermott said. “[Bookman’s piece] wasn’t just a standard breaking news item — it was the culmination of months of meticulous accountability reporting,” McDermott added. On the audience side, McDermott said that, in addition to a boost from NHPR’s partners at NPR and Google News, the chief justice story benefited from X (formerly known as Twitter). A post by NHPR president and CEO Jim Schachter caught on and inspired “a stream of supportive comments about the importance of local journalism.” BREAKING: Fearless reporting by New Hampshire Public Radio results in the resignation of the chief justice of the New Hampshire Supreme Court. #NHPolitics https://t.co/6DtIeEIwdp — Jim Schachter (@jimschachter) September 15, 2026 WBUR, one of two Boston-based public media stations, grew every month this quarter, moving from 1.45 million visits to 2.1 million in September, according to Similarweb. WBUR had the biggest raw gain of any station in September. Tiffany Campbell, WBUR’s executive editor for digital audience and news, said organic search traffic and Google Discover helped. “We’ve been working on building out many referral streams,” Campbell said, “but in early September Google delivered a lot of organic search audience via a couple of strong stories.” “Our referral diversification aims to be less reliant on Google organic search but it’s also important to take advantage when it delivers,” she added. Those strong stories? An explainer on the insanity defense during jury deliberations in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial, results from the Massachusetts primary held on Sept. 1, and a Here & Now interview with Associated Press photographer Richard Drew — who took the “Falling Man” photo — on the 25th anniversary of 9/11. All three stories drew both local and national readers, Campbell said. Campbell credited the steady rise in traffic to “things we’re always doing: in-depth local coverage, comprehensive reporting on a closely watched election (which was an early indication of interest in the general election in November) and relevant enterprise reporting.” The Milwaukee-based WUWM was the fastest climber in the top 25 this quarter. The station nearly doubled its visits between June and September, rising in our ranking from No. 31 to No. 15. According to Similarweb, the station’s visits rose 32% in August and by another 17% in September. Michelle Maternowski, WUWM audience innovation manager, said the surge started with Wisconsin’s August 11 primary. “We published our Voter Guide in time for that and saw a decent amount come to our meet the candidate posts,” she said. Readers were especially interested in news and information on the lesser-known races. “We see lots of traffic to the down ballot, statewide races — like state treasurer and secretary of state.” And then there’s the gift that keeps on giving. Published in 2019, WUWM’s segment on the 150th birthday of the periodic table still ranks “really high in search results.” “I think once the school year started up again, a lot of students were searching their periodic tables,” Maternowski said. “It is very silly that this story continues to get so much traffic.” If you only look at the top 25 stations, you’ll miss some impressive jumps. The Salt Lake City-based KUER, for example, took the biggest leap in ranking of any station in July. The station’s visits rose 122% that month, according to Similarweb’s numbers. “The numbers don’t lie,” Jim Hill, digital manager in the KUER newsroom, confirmed. “July was a monster for us.” Hill had expected a “plateau or small retreat” after a record year in 2025 — which included the Charlie Kirk killing and a shooting at a No Kings Protest in Utah. Instead, the news site has been ahead of last year’s pace. Total users are up 19% over last year, even after attempts to filter out bots, and social media referrals falling by 54%. (Hill noted the station’s social media producer was laid off and that KUER is attempting to “pivot to video/reels.”) The station saw “some runaway Google Discover success” last year but, in 2026, clicks from Google Discover are “less than half” of its 2025 figures. Hill credited “engagement reporting and audience-valued topics” that have “kept audiences reading” despite the headwinds. KUER also grew its “owned” email audience and drove 34% more users to the website compared to 2025, according to Hill. All in all, July was “very hit-heavy,” Hill said. The top 10 stories — led by Donald Trump’s decision to dramatically shrink two Utah national monuments — accounted for 64% of the month’s views. The station also saw a major boost from NPR, including multiple stories from a week-long hearing in the Charlie Kirk case. “Our newsroom was the ground team for NPR, so the network highlighted web coverage nationally,” Hill said. Most of the audience came from outside Utah. Hill said NPR can be directly attributed for 32% of sessions, Google Search 14%, and Google News 13.5%. Two wildfire stories also gave major traffic boosts. But audiences especially loved hearing about Utah getting full-color specialty license plates. The story was KUER’s top Google Discover story in July and also got a significant bump (14% of visits) from Reddit. “We affectionately refer to stories like this as license plate news,” Hill said. “It always hits with the audience.” Sure enough, a second plate story, on Utah cracking down on the infamous “Montana loophole,” ended the month as the No. 2 Discover story. Like several public media sites on our list, election season provided a bump to NHPR. New Hampshire held its primary on Sept. 8 and the statewide public radio station saw a traffic boost from results pages and campaign coverage, said NHPR director of audience engagement Casey McDermott. She described September as a solid month, not an outlier.

“But what makes September an exceptionally cool case study is that it reflects two fundamentals at the heart of our mission: a commitment to fresh, local reporting and a renewed internal investment in digital publishing,” McDermott said.

“[Bookman’s piece] wasn’t just a standard breaking news item — it was the culmination of months of meticulous accountability reporting,” McDermott added.

On the audience side, McDermott said that, in addition to a boost from NHPR’s partners at NPR and Google News, the chief justice story benefited from X (formerly known as Twitter). A post by NHPR president and CEO Jim Schachter caught on and inspired “a stream of supportive comments about the importance of local journalism.”

BREAKING: Fearless reporting by New Hampshire Public Radio results in the resignation of the chief justice of the New Hampshire Supreme Court. #NHPolitics https://t.co/6DtIeEIwdp

— Jim Schachter (@jimschachter) September 15, 2026

WBUR, one of two Boston-based public media stations, grew every month this quarter, moving from 1.45 million visits to 2.1 million in September, according to Similarweb. WBUR had the biggest raw gain of any station in September.

Tiffany Campbell, WBUR’s executive editor for digital audience and news, said organic search traffic and Google Discover helped.

“We’ve been working on building out many referral streams,” Campbell said, “but in early September Google delivered a lot of organic search audience via a couple of strong stories.”

“Our referral diversification aims to be less reliant on Google organic search but it’s also important to take advantage when it delivers,” she added.

Those strong stories? An explainer on the insanity defense during jury deliberations in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial, results from the Massachusetts primary held on Sept. 1, and a Here & Now interview with Associated Press photographer Richard Drew — who took the “Falling Man” photo — on the 25th anniversary of 9/11. All three stories drew both local and national readers, Campbell said.

Campbell credited the steady rise in traffic to “things we’re always doing: in-depth local coverage, comprehensive reporting on a closely watched election (which was an early indication of interest in the general election in November) and relevant enterprise reporting.”

The Milwaukee-based WUWM was the fastest climber in the top 25 this quarter. The station nearly doubled its visits between June and September, rising in our ranking from No. 31 to No. 15.

According to Similarweb, the station’s visits rose 32% in August and by another 17% in September. Michelle Maternowski, WUWM audience innovation manager, said the surge started with Wisconsin’s August 11 primary.

“We published our Voter Guide in time for that and saw a decent amount come to our meet the candidate posts,” she said. Readers were especially interested in news and information on the lesser-known races. “We see lots of traffic to the down ballot, statewide races — like state treasurer and secretary of state.”

And then there’s the gift that keeps on giving. Published in 2019, WUWM’s segment on the 150th birthday of the periodic table still ranks “really high in search results.”

“I think once the school year started up again, a lot of students were searching their periodic tables,” Maternowski said. “It is very silly that this story continues to get so much traffic.”

If you only look at the top 25 stations, you’ll miss some impressive jumps. The Salt Lake City-based KUER, for example, took the biggest leap in ranking of any station in July. The station’s visits rose 122% that month, according to Similarweb’s numbers.

“The numbers don’t lie,” Jim Hill, digital manager in the KUER newsroom, confirmed. “July was a monster for us.”

Hill had expected a “plateau or small retreat” after a record year in 2025 — which included the Charlie Kirk killing and a shooting at a No Kings Protest in Utah.

Instead, the news site has been ahead of last year’s pace. Total users are up 19% over last year, even after attempts to filter out bots, and social media referrals falling by 54%. (Hill noted the station’s social media producer was laid off and that KUER is attempting to “pivot to video/reels.”) The station saw “some runaway Google Discover success” last year but, in 2026, clicks from Google Discover are “less than half” of its 2025 figures. Hill credited “engagement reporting and audience-valued topics” that have “kept audiences reading” despite the headwinds. KUER also grew its “owned” email audience and drove 34% more users to the website compared to 2025, according to Hill.

All in all, July was “very hit-heavy,” Hill said. The top 10 stories — led by Donald Trump’s decision to dramatically shrink two Utah national monuments — accounted for 64% of the month’s views. The station also saw a major boost from NPR, including multiple stories from a week-long hearing in the Charlie Kirk case.

“Our newsroom was the ground team for NPR, so the network highlighted web coverage nationally,” Hill said. Most of the audience came from outside Utah. Hill said NPR can be directly attributed for 32% of sessions, Google Search 14%, and Google News 13.5%.

Two wildfire stories also gave major traffic boosts. But audiences especially loved hearing about Utah getting full-color specialty license plates. The story was KUER’s top Google Discover story in July and also got a significant bump (14% of visits) from Reddit.

“We affectionately refer to stories like this as license plate news,” Hill said. “It always hits with the audience.”

Sure enough, a second plate story, on Utah cracking down on the infamous “Montana loophole,” ended the month as the No. 2 Discover story.

#7501. Software Engineer - AI Tooling Infrastructure at Supabase

Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

We’re looking for a Software Engineer, AI Tooling Infrastructure to join our AI Tooling team and help build and run the backend services behind Supabase’s AI products. The Supabase MCP server is one example of what the team runs in production, alongside the services that support agent skills and the dashboard assistant. You’ll work closely with the Platform, SRE, Auth, Billing and Edge Functions teams, and with the engineers on the AI Tooling team who build the product surfaces.

The AI Tooling team runs its own services in production and carries its own on-call. This role makes sure the services they use are reliable, correctly authorized and observable. It is a systems and infrastructure role rather than a product AI role, and it is not an SRE role. You will build and operate these systems, not only advise on them.

This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments, owns what they ship in production, and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions.

Build and operate the production backend services behind Supabase’s AI products, including the MCP server: deployment, scaling, configuration and release.

Take ownership of how those services are structured, including splitting or reshaping a service when that makes it safer to run and easier to change.

Define, measure and meet reliability targets for the services the team runs. Set SLOs with the SRE team, track error budgets, and use them to decide what to fix first.

Participate in the AI Tooling team on-call rotation, and be a first responder for incidents in those services. Investigate, fix, coordinate with other teams during incidents, and write the follow-ups and runbooks.

Work the AI Tooling team support queue alongside on-call, and turn recurring issues into fixes rather than repeated manual answers.

Own authentication and authorization for AI and agent clients: OAuth apps, scoped tokens, and permissions that make sense for agents as well as humans, including how we change or deprecate a permission without breaking existing integrations.

Own observability for the services the team runs: metrics, traces, logs, dashboards and alerts, so we find problems before customers do.

Handle capacity and abuse for agent traffic: rate limits, cost and safety controls, and behavior under load or when a dependency degrades.

Improve the architecture of the services the team owns as they grow, including splitting or reshaping a service when that makes it safer to run and easier to change.

Work with the Platform team on shared code, review ownership and release process, and with the SRE team on infrastructure, alerting and incident practice.

Contribute to the code of the AI Tooling team’s tools, such as the MCP server, where it affects reliability and security, in partnership with the engineers who own the product surface.

Have 5+ years of experience building and running backend services in production, and have carried on-call for them.

Write strong TypeScript or Go, and are comfortable working in the other.

Have designed and operated APIs with real consumers: versioning, error handling, rate limiting, and backwards-compatible change.

Know OAuth, OIDC, JWT and API authorization well enough to debug them in production and to explain where implementations commonly deviate from the spec.

Have a good understanding of PostgreSQL and relational databases.

Are comfortable with CI/CD, Docker and containerized deployments, and with infrastructure as code. Any tool is fine.

Can debug across services: follow a slow or failing request through several systems using metrics, traces and logs.

Communicate clearly in writing, work with a wide range of stakeholders, and thrive in async, globally distributed teams.

Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and moving quickly.

Pick your centre of gravity. We expect you to be deep in at least one of these, and to tell us which:

APIs and auth: You have designed permission models, token scopes or OAuth flows for third-party or machine clients, and you have migrated them without breaking users.

Operations: You have run production services yourself: carried the pager, written alerts and runbooks, used SLOs or similar to decide what to fix, and made shared systems less risky over time.

Gateways and distributed systems: You have built or run proxies or gateways, or debugged hard failures across services (retries, partial failures, upstream outages, fail-open vs fail-closed decisions), and you can reason about load and degradation.

Experience with agent tooling (MCP or similar), or serving traffic from AI agents and LLM clients.

Experience moving a service out of a larger codebase while keeping existing clients working.

Experience with Grafana, OpenTelemetry, Logflare or a similar observability stack, and real SLO work.

Open-source contributions, especially to Node.js, Go, TypeScript or API tooling.

We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F)

#7498. Federal funding for public media is coming back, one way or another. But is it time for a deeper rethink?

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Congressional Democrats will have to determine whether they want to revive the old system Donald Trump defunded or build something more attuned to today’s media ecosystem.

It was 318 days ago that the Corporation for Public Broadcasting — the primary funder of public media in the United States since 1967 — officially ceased to be, the victim of Republican budget cuts and years of attacks from Donald Trump. CPB is not “on pause” or “in hibernation” — it’s dead. As its final CEO Patricia Harrison put it: “CPB’s final act would be to protect the integrity of the public media system and democratic values by dissolving, rather than allowing the organization to remain defunded and vulnerable to additional attacks.”

You may have heard, however, that we had some elections in the U.S. recently, and the Republicans who defunded NPR and PBS will no longer control the House of Representatives or Senate as of January 3. In their place will be Congressional Democrats much more favorable to public media. So it seems quite likely that the federal government’s next budget will re-fund it rather than de-fund it.

But with CPB officially no more, Democrats will have a rare opportunity to rethink the system from scratch instead of just prescribing minor tweaks to funding levels. The media environment of 2027 will, it goes without saying, be radically different from 1967’s. Over-the-air broadcasting is no longer America’s dominant medium. The immensely profitable newspapers that were the bedrock of news back then are shells of their former selves. And what was once a highly localized information ecosystem has been thoroughly nationalized and globalized, with access to news increasingly determined by a few large tech platforms. Democrats could just revive the old LBJ-era model — but should they instead build something new?

These questions will dominate the next year of discourse around public media, and interested parties are already laying out plans. This morning, the Roosevelt Institute released a new white paper titled “Creating a New U.S. Public Media System: Normative Arguments and Policy Options.” Written by Penn professor (and past Nieman Lab contributor) Victor Pickard, it argues for a thorough reinvention:

Taken together, the 2025 federal defunding of American public media, the ongoing collapse of local journalism, growing media oligarchy, a multitude of social harms arising from unregulated platforms and AI technologies, and other political and economic challenges to our media and democracy demonstrate the need for robust public media systems. Fundamental flaws — especially its funding mechanisms — are baked into the historical U.S. public media model, and they must be structurally addressed. The current crisis presents a unique opportunity to create an entirely new kind of public media system based on a local “Public Media Center” model. Pickard lays out three core ideas: de-privatization, democratization, and localization. De-privatization means more thoroughly removing “public” media from the interests of the private sector. No more sponsorship messages from Monsanto or ExxonMobil, no more need to pitch corporations or beg listeners for the funds needed to pay reporters. Pickard wants the public media system to be entirely publicly funded, to the tune of roughly $30 billion a year. That would be a massive increase — almost 60×! — from the pre-Trump level of federal funding, which was around $500 million a year. Even if you include all non-federal sources of revenue, $30 billion would still represent a public media system 8 to 10 times larger than what exists today. (Pickard dreams big!) RELATED ARTICLEDo countries with better-funded public media also have healthier democracies? Of course they doJoshua BentonJanuary 24, 2022But the fact that $30 billion sounds enormous is mostly about how small U.S. public media has always been compared to its international peers. Before defunding, the U.S. spent roughly $3 per person per year on public media. Compare that to countries like Norway ($110), Finland ($101), Denmark ($93), the U.K. ($81), France ($76), Czechia ($60), Japan ($53), Australia ($36), and Canada ($27). If Pickard got his $30 billion wish, U.S. public media funding would sit at roughly $88 per capita — BBC territory, roughly speaking. But even getting to the level of Canada or Australia would mean a huge increase. By democratization, Pickard means confronting criticism that public media systems’ output often skews toward the interests of elites — either the incumbent government in a case like Viktor Orbán’s Hungary or the sort of “latte-sipping NPR liberals” that conservatives have inveighed against for decades: Endeavoring to democratize public media institutions, therefore, is not only ethically sound but also strategic: Democratization can help ensure bipartisan trust, structural resilience, and journalistic independence. Toward this aim, a public media system should not be public in name only but actually owned and controlled by local communities. To encourage trust and community investment, this collective ownership and governance must translate to public participation in all stages of media production and dissemination. In fact, public media institutions are often cross-ideological islands of trust in an otherwise dismal landscape. This trust in public media can be further deepened through direct public ownership and participation, perhaps through community action programs, participatory budgeting, or some similar bottom-up model of democratic governance. Local media bureaus — rotating oversight boards that are locally elected or randomly selected — could help ensure additional public accountability.

Pickard lays out three core ideas: de-privatization, democratization, and localization.

De-privatization means more thoroughly removing “public” media from the interests of the private sector. No more sponsorship messages from Monsanto or ExxonMobil, no more need to pitch corporations or beg listeners for the funds needed to pay reporters.

Pickard wants the public media system to be entirely publicly funded, to the tune of roughly $30 billion a year. That would be a massive increase — almost 60×! — from the pre-Trump level of federal funding, which was around $500 million a year. Even if you include all non-federal sources of revenue, $30 billion would still represent a public media system 8 to 10 times larger than what exists today. (Pickard dreams big!)

RELATED ARTICLEDo countries with better-funded public media also have healthier democracies? Of course they doJoshua BentonJanuary 24, 2022But the fact that $30 billion sounds enormous is mostly about how small U.S. public media has always been compared to its international peers. Before defunding, the U.S. spent roughly $3 per person per year on public media. Compare that to countries like Norway ($110), Finland ($101), Denmark ($93), the U.K. ($81), France ($76), Czechia ($60), Japan ($53), Australia ($36), and Canada ($27). If Pickard got his $30 billion wish, U.S. public media funding would sit at roughly $88 per capita — BBC territory, roughly speaking. But even getting to the level of Canada or Australia would mean a huge increase.

By democratization, Pickard means confronting criticism that public media systems’ output often skews toward the interests of elites — either the incumbent government in a case like Viktor Orbán’s Hungary or the sort of “latte-sipping NPR liberals” that conservatives have inveighed against for decades:

Endeavoring to democratize public media institutions, therefore, is not only ethically sound but also strategic: Democratization can help ensure bipartisan trust, structural resilience, and journalistic independence. Toward this aim, a public media system should not be public in name only but actually owned and controlled by local communities. To encourage trust and community investment, this collective ownership and governance must translate to public participation in all stages of media production and dissemination. In fact, public media institutions are often cross-ideological islands of trust in an otherwise dismal landscape.

This trust in public media can be further deepened through direct public ownership and participation, perhaps through community action programs, participatory budgeting, or some similar bottom-up model of democratic governance. Local media bureaus — rotating oversight boards that are locally elected or randomly selected — could help ensure additional public accountability.

And for Pickard, localization is a logical response to the de-localization of media that the internet hath wrought. Many public radio and TV stations primarily serve as distributors of national content, in large part because funding is nowhere near robust enough to create enough local programming to fill each day. And no matter how much you like Ken Burns or All Things Considered, sending the same programming nationwide can limit the range of a community’s residents who might be interested. He advocates pushing more control away from a federal-level entity like CPB and toward states, counties, and cities via block grants.

Pickard describes the nodes of this system as Public Media Centers: “multimedia hubs that are federally guaranteed but locally owned and democratically governed,” which “would provide journalism, broadcasting, digital media, and other information services based on community needs.”11“Public Media Centers” is also what Pickard called them in one of his first public articulations of the idea, in his 2021 prediction here at Nieman Lab. Some might be housed in existing public radio or TV stations, others in post offices or libraries. And individual communities would be able to determine which media formats work best for them, rather than being locked into the expensive broadcast infrastructure required to reach audiences in 1967.

I am obliged to note that there are a huge number of barriers to Pickard’s vision becoming reality. Most obviously: $30 billion a year is a lot of money. That’s around the annual budget of the federal school lunch program ($32 billion), FEMA ($32 billion), or NASA ($25 billion). Secondly, the commercial media industry would not sit quietly while the federal government funds an enormous new rival that doesn’t need to sell ads or subscriptions. (For context, the entire U.S. newspaper industry pulls in around $20 billion a year in revenue.) And American suspicion of “state-funded media” goes deep enough that I can’t imagine Democrats looking to retake the White House in 2028 deciding this is the hill to die on.

But the new Congress is still weeks away from convening, and the next federal fiscal year starts more than 10 months from now. This is the season for big dreams, for expanding the edges of the Overton window, and in that sense, Pickard’s ideas should give newly empowered policymakers a lot to think about.

#7496. Robots.txt Guide – Best Practices For Search & AI Crawlers via @sejournal, @vahandev

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.
